sources: U.S. National Park Service, Staying Safe Around Bears: "Bears can run as fast as a racehorse both uphill and down."; "Do NOT run, but if the bear follows, stop and hold your ground."; "Like dogs, they will chase fleeing animals."; "Do NOT climb a tree. Both grizzlies and black bears can climb trees."; "If you are attacked by a brown/grizzly bear, leave your pack on and PLAY DEAD. Lay flat on your stomach with your hands clasped behind your neck."; "Remain still until the bear leaves the area."; "Fighting back usually increases the intensity of such attacks. However, if the attack persists, fight back vigorously."; "If you are attacked by a black bear, DO NOT PLAY DEAD."; "Try to escape to a secure place such as a car or building."; "Concentrate your kicks and blows on the bear's face and muzzle."; "If any bear attacks you in your tent, or stalks you and then attacks, do NOT play dead; fight back!"; "there is no single strategy that will work in all situations and that guarantees safety"; https://www.nps.gov/subjects/bears/safety.htm
Glacier National Park, Bear Safety: "Do not run! Back away slowly."; https://www.nps.gov/glac/planyourvisit/bears.htm

U.S. National Park Service, Bear Spray and Firearms: "Keep your bear spray on a belt holster or on a chest holster at all times. Never keep it in your backpack while hiking"; "Only use your bear spray when the bear is charging or attacking you."; https://www.nps.gov/articles/bearsprayfirearms.htm

Alaska Department of Fish and Game, What you should know about Bear Spray (2025): "Remember, you have only about 7-9 seconds worth of spray in a can."; https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/static/species/livingwithwildlife/bears/pdfs/bear_spray_what_you_should_know.pdf

Alaska Department of Fish and Game and partners, A Framework for Bear Safety Messages in Alaska (2017): "If a defensive bear makes contact with you and knocks you to the ground ... Yellowstone National Park, Bear Management: "Since 1979, Yellowstone has hosted over 148 million visits. Yellowstone National Park, Safety: since 1970, "91% of the people injured by bears in Yellowstone were hiking alone or with only one hiking partner."; "Hike in groups of 3 or more people"; "After the bear leaves, wait several minutes before moving."; https://www.nps.gov/yell/planyourvisit/safety.htm
